frus1877/d216: Fish authorizes recognizing Porfirio Díaz once he has no important adversary in arms and is the actual ruler, partly so the United States can accept Mexico's claims installment from a government it acknowledges.
frus1895p1/d246: Olney's statement of practice for Alfaro's revolutionary government in Ecuador: full relations once the de facto government is established with the general consent of the people and is honoring international law and treaties.
frus1899/d792: Hay's one-line test for Castro's Venezuela: complete control by a de facto government capable of fulfilling international obligations; the Department will not judge its title.
frus1900/d530: The fullest early statement of the de facto rule (Colombia, 1900): control of the machinery of the state, assent of the people, no substantial resistance, and capacity to meet international obligations; meanwhile local authorities are held to protect American lives and property.
frus1907p2/d27: Recognition of Dávila's provisional government in Honduras once it was judged competent to perform international obligations and had taken steps to restore constitutional rule and provide for an election; the surrounding chapter shows the step was coordinated with Mexico.
frus1930v01/d375: Stimson's press statement recognizing the provisional governments of Argentina, Peru and Bolivia: de facto control, no active resistance, intention to meet international obligations and to hold elections; he distinguishes the Central American treaty rule as an exception.
frus1933v05/d502: Roosevelt's Warm Springs statement on Cuba: no recognition of a provisional government that lacks the clear support and approval of the Cuban people, because recognition there carried unusual material and moral weight.
frus1933v05/d508: The Department's two stated criteria for recognizing a Cuban government in 1933: popular support, and ability to maintain law and order; Welles judged Grau San Martín's government met neither.
frus1937v05/d340: The Legal Adviser's ruling after Vargas's 1937 self-coup in Brazil: a regime set up by coup needs some form of recognition, but a recognized government that overthrows its own constitution does not.
frus1969-76ve11p2/d34: Ambassador Hill tells the Argentine military weeks before the 1976 coup that U.S. policy is to recognize a government that effectively exercises power and discharges its international obligations.
frus1866p2/d498: Seward approves the minister's refusal to recognize the government forcibly established by Prado in Peru and forbids any step implying recognition.
frus1866p2/d502: Seward's settled policy: revolutions in republican states are not accepted until the people have adopted them by organic law.
frus1868p2/d499: Seward's fullest statement: the United States does not deny a right of revolution, but a government installed by force must be sanctioned by the formal acquiescence and acceptance of the people before recognition.
frus1907p2/d148: The U.S. delegate's report on the 1907 Central American Peace Conference, printing the Additional Convention whose Article I bars recognition of governments arising from a coup or revolution until freely elected representatives have constitutionally reorganized the country.
frus1913/d7: Wilson's March 1913 statement to the Latin American posts: cooperation only with governments resting on law and the consent of the governed, not on arbitrary or irregular force.
frus1913/d1028: The August 1913 terms offered to Huerta's Mexico: an armistice, an early and free election, Huerta not a candidate, and all parties bound by the result; the United States pledges to recognize an administration chosen that way.
frus1917/d378: Lansing's circular on Tinoco's coup in Costa Rica: no recognition or support for any government unless it is clearly shown to be elected by legal and constitutional means.
frus1917/d382: Tinoco is told that even if elected he will not be recognized.
frus1923v02/d345: Hughes announces that U.S. recognition of new governments in the five Central American republics will follow Article II of the 1923 General Treaty of Peace and Amity, to which the United States was not a party.
frus1931v02/d232: Stimson rules that Martínez's regime in El Salvador is barred from recognition by Article II of the 1923 treaty, both because it came to power by revolution and because he had been Minister of War.
frus1934v05/d257: The United States recognizes the Martínez government on 26 January 1934, the day after Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua did.
frus1936v05/d112: Hull's instruction and the enclosed memorandum: the United States will no longer be guided by Article II of the 1923 treaty, because its own parties had violated it without invoking it, and invoking it would be meddling.
frus1877/d226: Foster reports telling Mexico that recognition of Díaz waited on measures against cross-border raids and the repeal of the Zona Libre, and on evidence of his ability to meet obligations to American citizens.
frus1904/d227: The U.S. minister answers the Morales government's request for recognition with a condition: a pledge to honor all engagements made with the legation and with preceding administrations.
frus1914/d506: Bryan ties probable recognition of the Zamor government in Haiti to its popular basis and raises customs administration, lighthouses and the Môle Saint-Nicolas in the same instruction.
frus1914/d544: Recognition of Théodore in Haiti is made conditional on a commission empowered to give assurances on a customs convention, railroad and bank settlements, protection of foreign interests, and no lease of Haitian territory to a European power.
frus1921v02/d344: Hughes's public statement on Obregón's Mexico: recognition is subordinate to a treaty safeguarding property acquired before the 1917 constitution, and will take place concurrently with Mexico's binding itself to its international obligations.
frus1923v02/d488: The arranged sequence of 1923: renewal of relations announced on the strength of the Mexico City commissioners' agreements, followed by signature of the General and Special Claims Conventions.
frus1943v05/d486: Hull's statement on the Bolivian coup of December 1943: hemispheric security and the war effort come first, including whether influence unfriendly to the Allies played a part.
frus1943v05/d33: Resolution XXII of the Emergency Advisory Committee for Political Defense: for the duration of the war, no recognition of a government instituted by force before the American governments consult on whether it honors the inter-American defense undertakings.
frus1944v07/d403: All nineteen consulting republics refused recognition to the Bolivian junta, which the Department hails as a success of the consultative procedure.
frus1944v07/d227: Armour proposes a minimum anti-Axis program the Farrell regime in Argentina must carry out before recognition and argues that recognition, much desired by Perón's group, is a powerful instrument.
frus1944v07/d432: Hull's summary of Warren's report on Bolivia, June 1944: the MNR leaders had been removed from office, Axis firms expropriated and the core of Axis aliens expelled, and recognition would hasten cooperation between the provisional government and the traditional parties.
frus1945v09/d250: The program agreed at Blair House for Argentina: declare war on Germany and Japan, comply with the Final Act of Mexico City and sign it; recognition by the American governments would follow.
frus1948v09/d7: PPS/24, the Department's policy paper of March 1948: three factors (de facto control, ability and willingness to meet obligations, general acquiescence of the people), recognition implying no approval, and non-recognition not to be used as a political weapon except in extreme cases.
frus1948v09/d74: Resolution XXXV of the Bogotá conference: continuity of diplomatic relations is desirable and establishing or maintaining relations implies no judgment on a government's domestic policy.
frus1948v09/d115: Kennan applies PPS/24 to the Venezuelan junta of November 1948: no useful purpose in protracted withholding; recognize after an interval, while stating that the use of force for political change is deplorable.
frus1949v02/d457: Daniels weighs delay against prompt resumption of relations after the 1949 Paraguayan coup and concludes that suspension is a feeble sanction that has not produced representative government.
frus1949v02/d448: The criteria applied to Arias's Panama in 1949 after consultation: no outside intervention, a broad popular basis, no civil-liberties question, and intent to honor international commitments.
frus1952-54v04/d327: Acheson recommends continuing relations with Batista after the 1952 coup: complete control, popular acquiescence, and satisfactory statements on international obligations, private capital and curbing international communist activities.
frus1955-57v07/d465: Recognition of Colombia's military junta in 1957: welcomed by the people, firmly in control, committed to international obligations and to free presidential elections.
frus1958-60v05mSupp/es_d43: The note recognizing El Salvador's junta in December 1960, conditioned in its own text on the junta's assurances about the constitution, treaties, human rights and free elections.
frus1961-63v12/d417: Contingency plan before Peru's 1962 election: if the military imposed a government, publicly withhold recognition, suspend aid and recall the ambassador, in concert with Latin American states.
frus1961-63v12/d421: Ball reports that the sharp U.S. and Latin American reaction to the July 1962 coup moved Peru's junta on elections, civil rights and treatment of the previous government's leaders.
frus1961-63v12/d363: The December 1963 decision to recognize the Dominican and Honduran regimes: the objective of withholding recognition had been a prompt return to constitutionally elected government, and further leverage was judged virtually nil.
frus1964-68v31/d152: Recognition of Barrientos's junta in Bolivia, 1964: in control, unopposed, constitutional liberties restored, elections promised, and private pledges against communist influence and relations with Cuba.
frus1964-68v31/d135: Rostow on the 1966 Argentine coup: seek the usual assurances on international obligations, civil liberties and an early return to constitutional government before recognizing, but do not insist on an election date.
frus1964-68v31/d512: Oliver's reflection after Peru's 1968 coup: practice no longer fits the doctrine that a coup cuts all relations pending recognition; he proposes that a coup should change the level of relations rather than end them.
frus1969-76ve10/d14: Nixon at the National Security Council, October 1969: go for automatic recognition, which avoids judging whether regimes are good or bad.
frus1969-76ve16/d148: Press guidance after the 1973 Chilean coup: the United States has moved away from the concept of recognition toward deciding whether relations continue, avoiding the value judgments recognition implies.
frus1977-80v24/d137: Bolivia, 1978: the United States continues relations without addressing recognition and states that continuing relations implies neither approval nor disapproval, while noting the new government's stated intentions on human rights.
frus1977-80v24/d160: After García Meza's 1980 coup in Bolivia the interagency group adopts goals on human rights, narcotics and a return to democracy and a strategy to isolate the regime.
